submission.natural_language_explanation: N2592+ detects formal normative/documentary register - running text that sets out binding terms or requirements (software licences, EULAs, terms of service, contracts, statutes and MUST/SHALL specifications): it keys at token level on that register's word-initial formal vocabulary (' stip-', ' prec-', ' subsc-', ' command', ' permission', ' notice', ' License', ' agreement') and integrates the evidence across the passage. A 60-130 token licence, contract or terms paragraph therefore sits at a mean activation of 0.5-1.1 with peaks of 2.3-3.3, while same-length narrative, encyclopaedic, news, medical, academic and blog prose stays at mean 0.00-0.05 (peak <= 1.4) and non-binding rulebooks (a hiking club's rules, a recipe's 'must' steps) stay at 0.00-0.02; the scan's apparent trigger tokens ' without', ' and' and ' notice' are silent in ordinary prose, so what fires the neuron is the document register and not the token (about a third of the scan's very top tokens - ISO timestamps, camelCase and hyphen fragments, '@angular/platform-browser' - remain unexplained by this reading).

rival_explanations: It tracks formal or institutional English generally rather than binding terms, so a privacy policy, a corporate dividend announcement, a patent claim or a newspaper report of a court case should fire at the same level as a licence; measured means of 0.10-0.23 for those against 0.47-1.11 for licences argue against it, but it predicts the reviewer's formal-but-non-binding holdouts will fire.

It is a token detector for a fixed set of formal tokens (' stip', ' prec', ' subsc', ' command', ' permission', ' notice', ' License'), each firing at a fixed strength wherever it appears, with the paragraph pattern just their density; that predicts a licence rewritten in plain words falls silent, whereas plain-word licence clauses measured a mean of 0.48.

It is a word-completion/fragment neuron that fires on non-final subword pieces of long Latinate words (matching the Jacobian lens's promoted continuations 'ulate', 'onductor', 'ular'), so dense technical or medical vocabulary should fire it; a 139-token clinical paragraph dense in such words measured a mean of 0.011.

readings.explanation: N2592+ detects formal normative/documentary register - running text that sets out binding terms or requirements (software licences, EULAs, terms of service, contracts, statutes and MUST/SHALL specifications): it keys at token level on that register's word-initial formal vocabulary (' stip-', ' prec-', ' subsc-', ' command', ' permission', ' notice', ' License', ' agreement') and integrates the evidence across the passage. A 60-130 token licence, contract or terms paragraph therefore sits at a mean activation of 0.5-1.1 with peaks of 2.3-3.3, while same-length narrative, encyclopaedic, news, medical, academic and blog prose stays at mean 0.00-0.05 (peak <= 1.4) and non-binding rulebooks (a hiking club's rules, a recipe's 'must' steps) stay at 0.00-0.02; the scan's apparent trigger tokens ' without', ' and' and ' notice' are silent in ordinary prose, so what fires the neuron is the document register and not the token (about a third of the scan's very top tokens - ISO timestamps, camelCase and hyphen fragments, '@angular/platform-browser' - remain unexplained by this reading).

It tracks formal or institutional English generally rather than binding terms, so a privacy policy, a corporate dividend announcement, a patent claim or a newspaper report of a court case should fire at the same level as a licence; measured means of 0.10-0.23 for those against 0.47-1.11 for licences argue against it, but it predicts the reviewer's formal-but-non-binding holdouts will fire.

It is a token detector for a fixed set of formal tokens (' stip', ' prec', ' subsc', ' command', ' permission', ' notice', ' License'), each firing at a fixed strength wherever it appears, with the paragraph pattern just their density; that predicts a licence rewritten in plain words falls silent, whereas plain-word licence clauses measured a mean of 0.48.

It is a word-completion/fragment neuron that fires on non-final subword pieces of long Latinate words (matching the Jacobian lens's promoted continuations 'ulate', 'onductor', 'ular'), so dense technical or medical vocabulary should fire it; a 139-token clinical paragraph dense in such words measured a mean of 0.011.

verdict.notes: positive_holdout: 9/10 passed; hard_negative: 9/20 passed; counterfactual: 7/7 passed; lookahead_consistency: 1/1 passed. Failed gates: specificity, beats_confound_baseline.
